ch.ch-00-hero.title: CodeChronicles
ch.ch-00-hero.subtitle: The history of programming, relived.
ch.ch-00-hero.tagline: The history of programming is still being written.
ch.ch-00-hero.summary: An invitation to voyage to the origin of code and traverse the full evolution of programming toward the future.
ch.ch-01-before-code.title: Before the Code
ch.ch-01-before-code.subtitle: Ideas, algorithms, machines
ch.ch-01-before-code.tagline: Before computers existed, there were algorithms.
ch.ch-01-before-code.summary: Mechanical engines, blueprints, and the figure of Ada Lovelace emerge. The concept of programming was born long before physical computers.
ch.ch-02-machines.title: The Machines
ch.ch-02-machines.subtitle: Primitive mechanics and electronics
ch.ch-02-machines.tagline: The machine learned to follow instructions.
ch.ch-02-machines.summary: From electromagnetic relays and punched cards to the Z3 and programmable engines. Computation turns tangible and instruction-driven.
ch.ch-03-computers.title: The Computers
ch.ch-03-computers.subtitle: Electronic computing is born
ch.ch-03-computers.summary: Vacuum tubes, ENIAC, UNIVAC, and the von Neumann architecture. Electronic programming transitions from lab theory into an industry.
ch.ch-04-languages.title: The First Languages
ch.ch-04-languages.subtitle: From machine code to compilers
ch.ch-04-languages.summary: FORTRAN, LISP, COBOL, and early compilers. The concept of high-level programming languages as we know them is born.
ch.ch-05-systems.title: Systems & Structure
ch.ch-05-systems.subtitle: C, UNIX, structured programming
ch.ch-05-systems.tagline: The era of systems and structure.
ch.ch-05-systems.summary: C and UNIX transform programming: portable operating systems, disciplined structured code, and the foundations of modern software.
ch.ch-06-oop.title: The Objects
ch.ch-06-oop.subtitle: Object-oriented programming
ch.ch-06-oop.summary: Smalltalk and C++ popularize object-oriented programming, radically transforming how engineers model and reason about software.
ch.ch-07-modern.title: The Modern Era
ch.ch-07-modern.subtitle: Python, Java, Ruby
ch.ch-07-modern.tagline: Languages proliferated; each solving a distinct challenge.
ch.ch-07-modern.summary: An explosion of modern languages engineered for developer productivity. Programming became wonderfully diverse and accessible worldwide.
ch.ch-08-web.title: The Web
ch.ch-08-web.subtitle: JavaScript and the open web
ch.ch-08-web.tagline: The internet transformed into the Web.
ch.ch-08-web.summary: JavaScript, TypeScript, and the browser runtime transform software: code no longer lives solely on local hardware, but across the universal web.
ch.ch-09-systems.title: Modern Systems
ch.ch-09-systems.subtitle: Go, Rust, scale and safety
ch.ch-09-systems.tagline: New systems for an interconnected world.
ch.ch-09-systems.summary: Go and Rust respond to planet-scale cloud challenges: lightweight concurrency, uncompromising memory safety, and elegant simplicity.
ch.ch-10-ai.title: AI & Assisted Coding
ch.ch-10-ai.subtitle: Machines that write code
ch.ch-10-ai.tagline: Intelligence became part of the stack.
ch.ch-10-ai.summary: Deep learning and large language models fundamentally reshape how humans author and comprehend software: real-time AI-assisted synthesis.
ch.ch-11-future.title: The Future of Code
ch.ch-11-future.subtitle: Quantum, generative systems, new paradigms
ch.ch-11-future.tagline: What will programming become when machines forge code?
ch.ch-11-future.summary: A thoughtful and inspiring journey into what lies ahead: quantum computing, generative architectures, and natural intent interfaces.
ct.epilogue.head: Code Never Sleeps
ct.epilogue.body: Every line written today stands upon the shoulders of Lovelace, Turing, Hopper, and millions of pioneers. The next chapter is being written by you.
ct.section.artifacts.head: Showcase of artifacts, figures and languages
card.char.ada-lovelace.quote: The Analytical Engine weaves algebraic patterns, just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves.
card.char.alan-turing.quote: We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.
card.char.margaret-hamilton.quote: There was no second chance. We had to find a way.
card.char.grace-hopper.quote: The most dangerous phrase in the language is: We\
card.char.dennis-ritchie.quote: UNIX is basically a simple operating system, but you have to be a genius to understand the simplicity.
card.char.alan-kay.quote: The best way to predict the future is to invent it.
card.char.guido-van-rossum.quote: Code is read much more often than it is written.
card.char.linus-torvalds.quote: Talk is cheap. Show me the code.
card.char.geoffrey-hinton.quote: If you want to understand the brain, build one.
card.char.demis-hassabis.quote: Solve intelligence, and then use that to solve everything else.
card.lang.fortran-language.context: In the 1950s, coding meant hand-crafting machine instructions. FORTRAN was the first widely adopted high-level language, multiplying productivity.
card.lang.c-language.context: Created to rewrite Unix with true hardware portability. C combined low-level memory access with high-level structural clarity.
card.lang.smalltalk-language.context: At Xerox PARC, Smalltalk invented pure object-oriented design and laid the foundation for modern graphical user interfaces.
card.lang.python-language.context: With elegant readability, Python revolutionized scientific computing and became the global standard lingua franca of AI.
card.lang.javascript-language.context: Crafted in 10 days for Netscape, JavaScript evolved into the most ubiquitous universal runtime on Earth.
card.lang.rust-language.context: Engineered for uncompromising memory safety without a garbage collector, Rust redefines mission-critical systems programming.
card.lang.mojo-language.context: Combines Python usability with C speed, built from the ground up for hardware accelerators and AI inference.
card.lang.qsharp-language.context: Domain-specific language engineered to express quantum algorithms via gates, superposition, and entanglement.
card.machine.analytical-engine.desc: Blueprints for a general-purpose mechanical computer featuring a processing mill, memory store, and punched card control.
card.machine.eniac-machine.desc: The first electronic general-purpose computer, housing 18,000 vacuum tubes capable of 5,000 additions per second.
card.machine.pdp-11-machine.desc: Iconic minicomputer from Digital Equipment Corporation upon which Unix and C were forged.
card.machine.xerox-alto-machine.desc: First personal workstation featuring a bitmapped display, mouse pointer, graphical user interface, and Ethernet networking.
card.machine.ibm-pc-machine.desc: The open architecture standard that democratized computing across homes and enterprises worldwide.
card.machine.nvidia-tensor-hardware.desc: Massive parallel floating-point architecture and Tensor Cores powering modern frontier AI training and inference.
card.event.bernoulli-algorithm.title: The Bernoulli numbers algorithm
card.event.bernoulli-algorithm.desc: Ada Lovelace publishes Note G, containing the first program crafted for execution by an automated calculation engine.
card.event.turing-computable-numbers.des: Alan Turing introduces the Universal Machine, formally proving mathematical limits of mechanical computation.
card.event.first-computer-bug.title: The first literal computer bug
card.event.first-compiler.title: The first compiler (A-0)
card.event.first-compiler.desc: Grace Hopper demonstrates software can translate human mathematical pseudo-code into machine instructions.
card.event.apollo-guidance.title: The software that landed humans on the Moon
card.event.apollo-guidance.desc: Margaret Hamilton directs AGC engineering: its prioritized asynchronous architecture saved the Apollo 11 lunar touchdown.
card.event.smalltalk-parc.title: Birth of modern personal computing
card.event.smalltalk-parc.desc: Alan Kay and Xerox PARC engineers create Smalltalk, GUI windows, icons, and mouse pointers inspiring Apple and Microsoft.
card.event.java-launch.title: Write Once, Run Anywhere
card.event.java-launch.desc: Sun Microsystems unveils Java and the JVM, liberating software from operating system vendor lock-in.
card.event.world-wide-web.title: Birth of the World Wide Web
card.event.world-wide-web.desc: Tim Berners-Lee releases HTTP and HTML at CERN, linking world knowledge in a royalty-free global network.
card.event.linux-announcement.title: The Linux announcement & Open Source triumph
card.event.linux-announcement.desc: Linus Torvalds posts a humble message unveiling a free kernel that would grow to power servers, supercomputers, and phones.
card.event.alphago-victory.title: AlphaGo\
card.event.alphago-victory.desc: DeepMind proves deep reinforcement learning can master complex human intuition in the world\
card.event.quantum-supremacy.title: Quantum Computational Supremacy milestone
card.event.quantum-supremacy.desc: Superconducting processors execute in minutes a computation requiring millennia on the world\
ct.hero.chip1: Looms, Babbage and the first algorithm of 1843.
ct.hero.chip2: Turing, electromagnetic relays and the dawn of silicon.
ct.hero.chip3: Fortran, Lisp, COBOL and Grace Hopper\
ct.hero.chip4: C, Unix, objects and the software that holds the world.
hero.sub: A cinematic voyage across three centuries of intellect, algorithms, silicon, and abstraction.
hero.chapters.label: Quick index of historical eras
ct.narr.ch-01-before-code: Lovelace saw far beyond pure arithmetic: she intuited that any symbolic relationship—music, imagery, formal logic—could be manipulated if an engine operated according to systematic rules.
ct.narr.ch-02-machines: Electromagnetic relays opened and closed circuits in milliseconds, transforming Boolean mathematics into measurable electric current and breathing physical life into the first programmable computing.
ct.narr.ch-03-computers: Electronic computers replaced mechanical inertia with the flow of electrons through vacuum tubes, accelerating computation speeds ten-thousand-fold and giving birth to software engineering during critical missions like Apollo.
ct.narr.ch-04-languages: Compilers democratized programming: engineers no longer had to memorize binary sequences on punched cards; abstract human thought and mathematical notation were translated directly into executable software.
ct.narr.ch-05-systems: The Unix philosophy—modular programs doing one thing well, composable via pipes—coupled with the surgical efficiency of C, established the architectural covenant governing modern civilization\
ct.narr.ch-06-oop: At Xerox PARC, Alan Kay and his team conceptualized software as a digital biology of autonomous cells communicating through messages. From this leap sprang windows, mice, icons, and the object-oriented paradigm.
ct.narr.ch-07-modern: The 1990s sparked a Cambrian explosion of software: languages optimized for human productivity, write-once portability (Java\
ct.narr.ch-08-web: Conceived at CERN to link static research papers, the World Wide Web evolved into humanity\
ct.narr.ch-09-systems: Confronted with hyperscale datacenters and multi-core silicon, industry demanded a new paradigm: Go streamlined cloud concurrency via lightweight goroutines, while Rust eradicated memory errors without requiring a garbage collector.
ct.narr.ch-10-ai: Code is no longer exclusively an artisan craft of human typing. Deep neural networks and Transformer architectures comprehend complex semantic patterns, empowering humans and machines to converse in natural language and synthesize software in real time.
ct.narr.ch-11-future: From quantum processors operating through superposition and entanglement to formal mathematical verification and biological computing, the frontier of code prepares to solve challenges long considered mathematically insurmountable.

wb.04.head: The rebellion against ones and zeros: birth of the compiler.
wb.04.desc: Before 1954, programming meant patching physical cables or binary arrays. Compilers proved machines could translate human mathematical thought directly into silicon.
wb.04.m1.desc: John Backus supersedes assembly: direct translation of mathematical formulas into CPU instructions.
wb.04.m1.note: Proved high-level code could be just as performant as hand-tuned assembly.
wb.04.m2.desc: John McCarthy conceives lambda functions, automatic garbage collection, and symbolic tree data.
wb.04.m2.note: The language that founded artificial intelligence and functional programming.
wb.04.m3.desc: Code authored in English prose: the standard that powered world banking and commerce.
wb.04.m3.note: Invention of the first compiler in history (A-0) and widespread industry standardization.
wb.04.m4.desc: Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson forge the universal language powering modern operating systems.
wb.04.m4.note: The direct bedrock of Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, and iOS.
wb.04.m5.desc: Guido van Rossum champions human readability. Decades later, it becomes the lingua franca of machine learning.
wb.04.m5.note: The bridge connecting mathematical algorithms to frontier models.
wb.comp.head: One problem, opposing philosophies.
wb.comp.desc: Compare how each generation conquered identical logic challenges through distinct paradigms: imperative, object-oriented, functional, and modern.
wb.06.tag: 06.B — The Xerox PARC Manifesto & Software Biology
wb.06.head: Everything is an object. Everything communicates via messages.
wb.06.desc: On the Xerox Alto, Alan Kay and Adele Goldberg replaced detached data procedures with autonomous digital organisms responding to messages. Observe original Smalltalk-80 code:
wb.06.lineage.head: The lineage of objects.
wb.06.lineage.desc: How the cellular metaphor conquered the software industry:
wb.06.l1.desc: Birth of classes, subclasses, and inheritance to simulate physical systems.
wb.06.l2.desc: Pure conceptual design: numbers, windows, and methods are objects exchanging messages.
wb.06.l3.desc: Classes infused into C: the expressive power of objects with zero runtime performance penalties.
wb.06.l4.desc: Type safety, garbage collection, and write-once run-anywhere execution on the JVM.

wb.08.desc: Source code of the very first web page published by Tim Berners-Lee on his CERN NeXT computer in 1991. A modest markup that altered human civilization:

wb.08.e3.desc: Blazing JIT compilation: JavaScript breaks free from browsers to dominate cloud server infrastructure.
wb.08.e4.desc: Static typing at hyperscale over JavaScript: foundation of the most intricate web apps in history.

wb.10.m2.desc: Gradient backpropagation algorithm unlocking scalable multi-layer deep network training.
wb.10.m3.desc: Shedding recurrence: parallelized attention across arbitrary sequence lengths.
wb.10.m4.desc: Assisted programming: software creation as fluid dialogue between humans and frontier models.
